The Politics & the Pendulum

American voters keep handing power to one party, growing tired of it, and handing it back. This page puts the cartoon of that cycle next to a century of measurable policy, so we can test where the metaphor holds and where it breaks.

I. The cycle, annotated

Tap a numbered marker
    Marker 3, a closer look

    What does the dog do with the car, now that it finally caught it?

    Shel Silverstein asked the same question in “The Search,” from Where the Sidewalk Ends (1974). His narrator hunts and hunts for the pot of gold at the rainbow's end, finally finds it half-hidden in the grass under a crooked branch, and in the moment of triumph is left wondering what there is to look for next.

    That is the hinge between stages 2 and 3. A campaign runs on the chase: a clear opponent, a short list of promises, a crowd. Victory removes all three. Winners then face budgets, courts, divided Congresses and their own coalition's competing wishes. Both parties have lived it: House Republicans after their 1994 sweep, Democrats after the 2008 wave, each losing ground at the next turn of the cycle. Section II shows what each administration actually did once it caught the car.

    For discussion: is the letdown after winning a flaw in our politics, or the thermostat doing its job?

    III. What the record says about the pendulum

    For discussion

    Where it holds

    The swing in who governs is real. Since 1952, a party has kept the White House for more than eight straight years only once (1981–1993). The president's party has lost House seats in every midterm since 1934 except 1934, 1998 and 2002.

    On the top tax rate, every change since 1993 has moved with the party in power: up under Clinton (1993) and Obama (2013), down under George W. Bush (2001–03) and Trump (2018).

    Where it breaks

    A pendulum returns to the same place. American policy does not. The top rate fell from 91% to the 28–40% band and has stayed there under both parties. Spending's biggest jumps came from crises (World War II, 2009, 2020), not from which party won.

    Programs ratchet. Eisenhower kept the New Deal, Reagan signed a Social Security rescue, Clinton signed welfare reform. The pivot point itself moves.

    What scholars call it

    Thermostatic opinion (Wlezien, 1995): the public asks for less when policy moves left and more when it moves right. Stimson and colleagues find this works best on issues where party positions are clear.

    Cycles of history (Arthur Schlesinger Jr., 1986): roughly 30-year swings between eras of public purpose and private interest. A useful frame, and a contested one.

    Sources: top marginal individual income tax rates, Tax Policy Center, “Historical Highest Marginal Income Tax Rates” (IRS, Pechman, Steuerle, JCT). Federal net outlays as % of GDP, OMB via FRED series FYONGDA188S (1929 onward; earlier years not in the series). Thermostatic model: Wlezien (1995); Coggins, Stimson, Atkinson & Baumgartner, The Dynamics of Public Opinion (Cambridge, 2022). Top rate ignores income thresholds, surtaxes and deductions; 1944–63 figures were subject to maximum effective-rate caps. Bands follow inauguration dates; policy effects often lag a year or more and depend on which party held Congress.
